claims.source: Similar to sea urchin and mammalian cilia and flagella, the shape of the S. rosetta radial spoke heads resemble narrow ice skates (Figure 3C'and F; Figure 4), rather than the broad radial spoke head morphology of other unicellular species like Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena (Figure 4; Barber et al., 2012; Grossman-Haham et al., 2021; Gui et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2014; Pigino et al., 2011; Pigino et al., 2012; Poghosyan et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 4, and citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: The radial spoke head morphology of Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena is broad.
claims.source: Similar to sea urchin and mammalian cilia and flagella, the shape of the S. rosetta radial spoke heads resemble narrow ice skates (Figure 3C'and F; Figure 4), rather than the broad radial spoke head morphology of other unicellular species like Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena (Figure 4; Barber et al., 2012; Grossman-Haham et al., 2021; Gui et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2014; Pigino et al., 2011; Pigino et al., 2012; Poghosyan et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4 and citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: The head domains of S. rosetta RS1 and RS2 are separated from one another.
claims.source: The head domains of S. rosetta RS1 and RS2 are separated from one another, whereas those of RS2 and RS3 are connected (Figure 3C, E, and F, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claims.claim: The head domains of S. rosetta RS2 and RS3 are connected.
claims.source: The head domains of S. rosetta RS1 and RS2 are separated from one another, whereas those of RS2 and RS3 are connected (Figure 3C, E, and F, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claims.claim: Many conserved MIP structures were identified within the S. rosetta flagellar doublet microtubules, including MIPs 1a, 1b, 2a, 2b, 2c, 3a, 3b, and 6a-d.
claims.source: Based on their locations and periodicities along the 96 nm repeat, we identified many conserved MIP structures within the S. rosetta flagellar doublet microtubules, including MIPs 1 a, 1b, 2 a, 2b, 2 c, 3 a, 3b, and 6a-d (Figure 5, A-F).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: In S. rosetta, MIP1a is shorter than MIP1b.
claims.source: MIP1a is typically longer than MIP1b in other species (Song et al., 2020), but in S. rosetta, MIP1a is shorter than MIP1b (Figure 5, A-B, D-E).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5 and citation to Song et al., 2020.

claims.claim: A previously unobserved ~3.5 nm wide filamentous MIP, named rail-MIP, was identified in S. rosetta flagella.
claims.source: Furthermore, we identified a previously unobserved ~3.5 nm wide filamentous MIP, here named rail-MIP, which runs along the length of the A-tubule near protofilament A13 and seems to connect to MIP 6ab (Figure 5A and G, class 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The rail-MIP runs along the length of the A-tubule near protofilament A13 and seems to connect to MIP 6ab.
claims.source: Furthermore, we identified a previously unobserved ~3.5 nm wide filamentous MIP, here named rail-MIP, which runs along the length of the A-tubule near protofilament A13 and seems to connect to MIP 6ab (Figure 5A and G, class 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The rail-MIP was present in only 39% of all averaged axonemal repeat units.
claims.source: Indeed, these analyses revealed that the rail-MIP was not ubiquitously present: only 39% of all averaged axonemal repeat units contained the rail-MIP, and its presence was enriched in DMTs 5–7 (Figure 5G, class 2 and table), as compared to doublets 1–4 and 8–9, which mostly lacked the rail-MIP (Figure 5G, class 1 and table).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: The presence of rail-MIP was enriched in DMTs 5-7.
claims.source: Indeed, these analyses revealed that the rail-MIP was not ubiquitously present: only 39% of all averaged axonemal repeat units contained the rail-MIP, and its presence was enriched in DMTs 5–7 (Figure 5G, class 2 and table), as compared to doublets 1–4 and 8–9, which mostly lacked the rail-MIP (Figure 5G, class 1 and table).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: The rail-MIP is present in a cryo-FIB-milled lamella containing the proximal region of the flagellum.
claims.source: This asymmetric distribution does not appear to correlate with any other observed features (such as presence of vane, barbs, microvilli, or IFT particles), but the rail-MIP is present in a cryo-FIB-milled lamella containing the proximal region of the flagellum (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that its distribution could be related to the location of the tomogram along the length of the flagellum (proximal vs. distal).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The rail-MIP distribution could be related to the location of the tomogram along the length of the flagellum (proximal vs. distal).
claims.source: This asymmetric distribution does not appear to correlate with any other observed features (such as presence of vane, barbs, microvilli, or IFT particles), but the rail-MIP is present in a cryo-FIB-milled lamella containing the proximal region of the flagellum (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that its distribution could be related to the location of the tomogram along the length of the flagellum (proximal vs. distal).
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the observed distribution pattern.

claims.claim: S. rosetta flagellar DMTs contain one ~4 nm long hole per axonemal repeat in the inner junction between protofilaments A1 and B10.
claims.source: Flagellar DMTs of most (wild-type) species described so far by cryo-ET display one ~4 nm long hole per axonemal repeat in the inner junction between protofilaments A1 and B10; the only described exception is the T. brucei flagellar DMTs that has an additional (more proximal) inner junction hole per repeat (Imhof et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Imhof et al., 2019 and established knowledge from cryo-ET studies.

claims.claim: One PACRG-subunit is missing near the N-DRC base-plate from the FAP20-PACRG inner junction filament.
claims.source: We and others have shown that one PACRG-subunit is missing near the N-DRC base-plate from the FAP20-PACRG inner junction filament (Dymek et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2019; Nicastro et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Dymek et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2019; Nicastro et al., 2011.

claims.claim: S. rosetta flagella contain two additional inner junction-holes, one near the base of RS1, and one near the base of RS3.
claims.source: In addition to this inner junction-hole near the N-DRC, S. rosetta flagella contain two additional inner junction-holes, one near the base of RS1, and one near the base of RS3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and D, pink and green arrowheads).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The additional inner junction holes in S. rosetta could represent additional PACRG subunit losses.
claims.source: Distances between the previously-reported N-DRC-related inner junction-hole and the additional proximal and distal hole are ~32 and~16 nm, respectively, suggesting that they could represent additional PACRG subunit losses, given the 8 nm periodicity of the FAP20-PACRG repeat (Dymek et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Based on inference from measured distances and citation to Dymek et al., 2019.

claims.claim: S. rosetta flagellar DMTs exhibit a ~6.5 nm long gap in protofilament A2 of the A-tubule between RS3 and RS1 from the next axonemal repeat unit, likely due to a missing tubulin dimer.
claims.source: S. rosetta flagellar DMTs also exhibit a (so far unique)~6.5 nm long gap in protofilament A2 of the A-tubule between RS3 and RS1 from the next axonemal repeat unit, likely due to a missing tubulin dimer (Figure 5H, class 2; Figure 5—figure supplement 3, B and D, olive arrowheads).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3, with inference about the cause.

claims.claim: The A2-hole is present in ~39% of repeats in S. rosetta flagella.
claims.source: Our classification analyses revealed that the A2-hole is present in ~39% of repeats, including over 50% of repeats from DMTs 1, 5, and 6 and with lower frequencies in the other DMTs (Figure 5H table: class 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: The S. rosetta CPC has a relatively fixed orientation.
claims.source: Like other opisthokonts, the S. rosetta CPC has a relatively fixed orientation, and the plane that contains both CPC microtubules is roughly parallel to the 5–6 bridge (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and comparison to other opisthokonts.

claims.claim: The plane containing both CPC microtubules in S. rosetta is roughly parallel to the 5-6 bridge.
claims.source: Like other opisthokonts, the S. rosetta CPC has a relatively fixed orientation, and the plane that contains both CPC microtubules is roughly parallel to the 5–6 bridge (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: S. rosetta's flagellum has a planar, sinusoidal waveform with an amplitude perpendicular to the CPC and 5-6-bridge planes.
claims.source: This orientation is consistent with S. rosetta's flagellum having a planar, sinusoidal waveform (Dayel et al., 2011; Dayel and King, 2014) with an amplitude (beating direction) that is perpendicular to the CPC and 5–6-bridge planes.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Dayel et al., 2011 and Dayel and King, 2014, and inference from CPC orientation.

claims.claim: Subtomogram averaging of >1300 CPC repeats from 28 cryo-tomograms yielded an average with 2.5 nm resolution.
claims.source: To better resolve the molecular details of the S. rosetta CPC, we performed subtomogram averaging of >1300 repeats (32 nm length) that were extracted from 28 cryo-tomograms (selected based on best image signal-to-noise ratio) (Figure 6), which yielded an average with 2.5 nm resolution (0.5 FSC criterion) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures and Table 1.

claims.claim: The S. rosetta CPC contains all major projections described in other organisms with longitudinal periodicities of 16 nm (C1a, b; C2a, b, c, d, and e) and 32 nm (C1c, d, e, f).
claims.source: The S. rosetta CPC contains all major projections described in other organisms with the previously described longitudinal periodicities of 16 nm (C1a, b; C2a, b, c, d, and e) and 32 nm (C1c, d, e, f) (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2; Carbajal-González et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citations to Carbajal-González et al., 2013 and Fu et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The S. rosetta CPC strongly resembles that of sea urchin sperm flagella.
claims.source: In many ways, the S. rosetta CPC strongly resembles that of sea urchin sperm flagella (Carbajal-González et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2019): both lack the C2 MIP, have a small C1e projection, and exhibit prominent connections between the C1a and C2a projections, as compared to the Chlamydomonas CPC (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citations to Carbajal-González et al., 2013 and Fu et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Both S. rosetta and sea urchin CPCs lack the C2 MIP.
claims.source: In many ways, the S. rosetta CPC strongly resembles that of sea urchin sperm flagella (Carbajal-González et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2019): both lack the C2 MIP, have a small C1e projection, and exhibit prominent connections between the C1a and C2a projections, as compared to the Chlamydomonas CPC (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citations to Carbajal-González et al., 2013 and Fu et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Both S. rosetta and sea urchin CPCs have a small C1e projection.
claims.source: In many ways, the S. rosetta CPC strongly resembles that of sea urchin sperm flagella (Carbajal-González et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2019): both lack the C2 MIP, have a small C1e projection, and exhibit prominent connections between the C1a and C2a projections, as compared to the Chlamydomonas CPC (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citations to Carbajal-González et al., 2013 and Fu et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Both S. rosetta and sea urchin CPCs exhibit prominent connections between the C1a and C2a projections.
claims.source: In many ways, the S. rosetta CPC strongly resembles that of sea urchin sperm flagella (Carbajal-González et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2019): both lack the C2 MIP, have a small C1e projection, and exhibit prominent connections between the C1a and C2a projections, as compared to the Chlamydomonas CPC (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citations to Carbajal-González et al., 2013 and Fu et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The S. rosetta CPC exhibits partial reduction of the C1d protein network, specifically it seems that FAP54 is lacking.
claims.source: One unique feature of the S. rosetta CPC, however, is the partial reduction of the C1d protein network, specifically it seems that FAP54 is lacking (Han et al., 2022), which exposes a larger area of the C1 microtubule wall (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citation to Han et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Vane filaments were clearly observed extending from the flagellar membrane on either side of the S. rosetta flagellum.
claims.source: In contrast to previous studies in which vane preservation was an issue, we clearly observed vane filaments extending from the flagellar membrane on either side of the flagellum in S. rosetta, both in the cryo-FIB lamella of the proximal flagellar region (Figure 2, D and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), as well as more distally, where the flagellum is embedded in ice thin enough to be directly imaged using cryo-ET (Figure 2G, Figure 7).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: The vane originates at the base of the flagellum.
claims.source: The vane originates at the base of the flagellum, and its edges often extend the entire width of (and beyond) our tomograms and lamella, which are ~1.2 µm (tomograms) to ~3 µm (lamella) wide (Figure 2D–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: The vane edges often extend the entire width of (and beyond) the tomograms and lamella.
claims.source: The vane originates at the base of the flagellum, and its edges often extend the entire width of (and beyond) our tomograms and lamella, which are ~1.2 µm (tomograms) to ~3 µm (lamella) wide (Figure 2D–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: The plane containing the vane appears to be oriented parallel to the ice layer in which the sample is embedded, likely due to surface tension forces during blotting.
claims.source: In our data, the plane containing the vane varies in relation to the CPC/sub-5–6 planes, and instead appears to be oriented parallel to the ice layer in which the sample is embedded, likely due to surface tension forces during blotting (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J-K).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J-K and inference about the cause.

claims.claim: The vane orientation is consistent with its predicted physiological function in the pumping mechanism of filter feeders.
claims.source: This orientation is consistent with the vane's predicted physiological function in the pumping mechanism of these filter feeders (Nielsen et al., 2017), as the vane would be naturally positioned to experience hydrodynamic drag, pushing liquid and prey close to the collar (Figure 6—figure supplement 1L).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Nielsen et al., 2017 and inference from observed orientation.

claims.claim: The S. rosetta flagellar vane is composed of two sheets of thin filaments on either side of the flagellum.
claims.source: Our data suggest that the S. rosetta flagellar vane is composed of two sheets of thin filaments on either side of the flagellum, which extend from the flagellar membrane for approximately 80 nm before they split and attach to neighboring filaments to form diamond-shaped meshes (Figure 7A-D).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claims.claim: Vane filaments extend from the flagellar membrane for approximately 80 nm before they split and attach to neighboring filaments to form diamond-shaped meshes.
claims.source: Our data suggest that the S. rosetta flagellar vane is composed of two sheets of thin filaments on either side of the flagellum, which extend from the flagellar membrane for approximately 80 nm before they split and attach to neighboring filaments to form diamond-shaped meshes (Figure 7A-D).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claims.claim: One or two rows of 'nodes' are visible near the flagellar membrane where the vane filaments first branch.
claims.source: One or two rows of 'nodes' are visible near the flagellar membrane where the filaments first branch (Figure 2F, Figure 7A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: The two sheets of vane filaments and the nodes are separated by ~45 nm.
claims.source: Because our reconstructions are three dimensional, we can view these nodes rotated 90 degrees around the x-axis, which clearly shows that the two sheets of vane filaments and the nodes are separated by ~45 nm (Figure 7A, inset).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A inset.

claims.claim: The nodes of the vane filaments are offset from one another so that the vertices of the diamonds from one sheet are centered within the diamonds from the overlaying sheet when viewed from top down.
claims.source: The nodes of the vane filaments are offset from one another so that the vertices of the diamonds from one sheet are centered within the diamonds from the overlaying sheet when viewed from top down (Figure 7A and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A and C.

claims.claim: Some regions of S. rosetta flagella have vane filaments that are highly organized and interconnected, whereas others have wispy, individual filaments.
claims.source: Consistent with previous reports, we observed some regions with vane filaments that were highly organized and interconnected, whereas others appeared to have wispy, individual filaments (Figure 7B-D).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claims.claim: Vane filaments were apparent in all but one of the 54 tomograms analyzed.
claims.source: Vane filaments were apparent in all but one of the 54 tomograms we analyzed, with most tomograms exhibiting at least partial organized, mesh-like structures (Figure 7B–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claims.claim: Vane filaments were observed within the flagellar pocket at the base of the flagellum.
claims.source: We also observed vane filaments within the flagellar pocket at the base of the flagellum (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Previously undescribed barb-like membrane complexes extend ~50 nm from the extracellular surface of the S. rosetta flagellar membrane.
claims.source: In regions of the flagellar membrane adjacent to where the vane filaments protrude, we also observed previously undescribed barb-like membrane complexes, hereafter denoted as 'barbs', that extend ~50 nm from the extracellular surface of the flagellar membrane (Figure 7E-I).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7E-I.

claims.claim: Subtomogram averaging of 600 barb particles with fourfold symmetry yielded an average with 2.5 nm resolution.
claims.source: To better resolve the molecular details of these barbs, we performed subtomogram averaging and applied fourfold symmetry resulting in 600 averaged particles that yielded an average with 2.5 nm resolution (0.5 FSC criterion) (Figure 7F–I; Table 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures and Table 1.

claims.claim: The barbs consist of a top knob and a central rod with a wider mid-body, from which four arms protrude to connect to the membrane.
claims.source: The barbs consist of a top knob and a central rod with a wider mid-body, from which four arms protrude to connect to the membrane (Figure 7E-I).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7E-I.

claims.claim: The number of barbs varied greatly between tomograms, ranging from 0 to 22 barbs.
claims.source: The number of barbs varied greatly between tomograms (which show ~2 µm flagellar length), ranging from 0 to 22 barbs, but their location was consistently near the base of the vane filaments, with a median distance of 50 nm from the barb structures to the vane plane (Figure 7I–K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–I).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7I-K and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-I.

claims.claim: Barb location was consistently near the base of the vane filaments, with a median distance of 50 nm from the barb structures to the vane plane.
claims.source: The number of barbs varied greatly between tomograms (which show ~2 µm flagellar length), ranging from 0 to 22 barbs, but their location was consistently near the base of the vane filaments, with a median distance of 50 nm from the barb structures to the vane plane (Figure 7I–K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–I).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7I-K and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-I.

claims.claim: A lumen is visible throughout parts of the central rod of the barbs, but the cavity/channel does not appear to be continuous.
claims.source: Although a lumen is visible throughout parts of the central rod, the cavity/channel does not appear to be continuous, and the base of the rod seems only weakly connected to the membrane, if at all.
claims.evidence: Based on observation of the barb structure.

claims.claim: The base of the barb rod seems only weakly connected to the membrane, if at all.
claims.source: Although a lumen is visible throughout parts of the central rod, the cavity/channel does not appear to be continuous, and the base of the rod seems only weakly connected to the membrane, if at all.
claims.evidence: Based on observation of the barb structure.

claims.claim: Several barb-like structures were observed within the flagellar pocket.
claims.source: We also observed several barb-like structures within the flagellar pocket (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Barb structures were not observed on the surface of 3D reconstructed E. pacifica bacterial cells.
claims.source: The overall shape of the barbs resembles head-less bacteriophages or bacterial secretion needles, but barb structures were not observed on the surface of 3D reconstructed E. pacifica bacterial cells, which were co-cultured with S. rosetta as a food source (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-C.

claims.claim: The structure and organization of the dyneins, radial spokes, and the CPC observed for metazoan flagella are consistent with those of the unicellular choanoflagellate S. rosetta.
claims.source: Here, we find that the structure and organization of the dyneins, radial spokes, and the CPC observed for metazoan flagella are consistent with those of the unicellular choanoflagellate S. rosetta.
claims.evidence: Based on comparison of data from this study with known metazoan structures.

claims.claim: The structural features of dyneins, radial spokes, and CPC were likely present in the urchoanozoan, pre-dating the transition to multicellularity.
claims.source: This suggests that these changes were likely present in the urchoanozoan (the phylogenetic group containing all Choanoflagellates and metazoans), pre-dating the transition to multicellularity.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the observed similarities between S. rosetta and metazoans.

claims.claim: Most unicellular species contain three outer dynein heads per ODA, whereas flagella from multicellular species typically contain only two.
claims.source: Most unicellular species contain three outer dynein heads (i.e. three dynein heavy chains) per ODA, whereas flagella from multicellular species typically contain only two (Lin et al., 2014; Nicastro et al., 2006; Pigino et al., 2012; Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Lin et al., 2014; Nicastro et al., 2006; Pigino et al., 2012 and data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The third outer dynein heavy chain was lost in metazoans and most likely independently in excavates.
claims.source: This is consistent with comparative genomic data suggesting that the third outer dynein heavy chain was lost in metazoans and – most likely independently – in excavates (Kollmar, 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kollmar, 2016.

claims.claim: Unicellular organisms like Tetrahymena and Chlamydomonas have broad RS head structures and connections between all three radial spoke heads.
claims.source: In addition, unicellular organisms like Tetrahymena and Chlamydomonas have broad RS head structures and connections between all three radial spoke heads, whereas metazoan RS head structures are narrow, RS1 and RS2 are reduced to a pair of thin blades, and RS1 and RS2 are clearly separated from one another (Figure 4; Grossman-Haham et al., 2021; Gui et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4 and citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: Metazoan RS head structures are narrow, RS1 and RS2 are reduced to a pair of thin blades, and RS1 and RS2 are clearly separated from one another.
claims.source: In addition, unicellular organisms like Tetrahymena and Chlamydomonas have broad RS head structures and connections between all three radial spoke heads, whereas metazoan RS head structures are narrow, RS1 and RS2 are reduced to a pair of thin blades, and RS1 and RS2 are clearly separated from one another (Figure 4; Grossman-Haham et al., 2021; Gui et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4 and citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: The CPC orientation is fixed in metazoans, with stable connections between C1a and C2a and a reduced C1e projection.
claims.source: Furthermore, the CPC orientation is fixed in metazoans, with stable connections between C1a and C2a and a reduced C1e projection (Carbajal-González et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Carbajal-González et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Loss of bulkier flagellar structures may have generated space to accommodate additional molecular components in the common ancestor of choanoflagellates and animals.
claims.source: We can speculate that loss of bulkier flagellar structures like the third outer dynein head, broad radial spoke heads, and larger CPC projections may have generated space to accommodate additional molecular components in the common ancestor of choanoflagellates and animals.
claims.evidence: Based on speculation about evolutionary advantages.

claims.claim: Cilia and flagella in animals have adapted many additional signaling functions and molecules compared to free-swimming unicellular eukaryotes like Chlamydomonas.
claims.source: Although free-swimming unicellular eukaryotes like Chlamydomonas also signal through their flagella (sensing light, chemical environmental cues, and mechanosensory stimuli), cilia and flagella in animals have adapted many additional signaling functions and molecules, including T2R, progesterone receptors, estrogen receptor-ß, interleukin-6 receptor, and Hedgehog (HH) pathway components (Bloodgood, 2010; Mitchell, 2007; Sigg et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Bloodgood, 2010; Mitchell, 2007; Sigg et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The reduced RS head structures, CPC projections, and dynein motors in S. rosetta could be related to a shift away from predator avoidance toward increased signaling functions in a more stable and protected environment.
claims.source: Could the reduced RS head structures, CPC projections, and dynein motors in S. rosetta be related to a shift away from predator avoidance toward increased signaling functions in a more stable and protected environment?
claims.evidence: Based on speculation about evolutionary pressures.

claims.claim: The additional force provided by three outer dynein arm motors could help counteract the hydrodynamic effects of multiple cilia and flagella in organisms like Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena.
claims.source: For example, the additional force provided by three outer dynein arm motors could help counteract the hydrodynamic effects of multiple cilia and flagella in organisms like Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena, whereas the evolutionary selection pressure to retain the third outer dynein head may be lost in organisms with only one flagellum.
claims.evidence: Based on speculation about functional advantages.

claims.claim: The evolutionary selection pressure to retain the third outer dynein head may be lost in organisms with only one flagellum.
claims.source: For example, the additional force provided by three outer dynein arm motors could help counteract the hydrodynamic effects of multiple cilia and flagella in organisms like Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena, whereas the evolutionary selection pressure to retain the third outer dynein head may be lost in organisms with only one flagellum.
claims.evidence: Based on speculation about evolutionary pressures.

claims.claim: A combination of the rail-MIP and A2-hole may provide the strength and flexibility necessary to compensate for the loss of bulkier flagellar structures in S. rosetta.
claims.source: We report a unique rail-MIP in S. rosetta flagella that runs the length of the A-tubule lumen. MIPs are thought to reinforce structural integrity of doublet microtubules (Owa et al., 2019), therefore a combination of the rail-MIP and A2-hole identified here may provide the strength and flexibility necessary to compensate for the loss of bulkier flagellar structures.

results.result: Choanoflagellates are the closest living unicellular relatives to metazoans, sharing a last common ancestor (the urchoanozoan) more than 600 million years ago.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature (Carr et al., 2008; King, 2004; Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008; Steenkamp et al., 2006), representing accepted phylogenetic knowledge.

results.result: S. rosetta cells contain a single flagellum with a 9+2 axonemal microtubule arrangement, surrounded by 25-36 actin-based microvilli, and use planar flagellar beating for motility and feeding.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6 are supported by both current imaging data (Figure 1) and prior literature (Dayel et al., 2011; Karpov, 2016; Karpov and Leadbeater, 1998; Pettitt et al., 2002), establishing basic S. rosetta flagellar architecture.

results.result: Cryo-FIB milling and cryo-ET successfully visualized the S. rosetta basal apparatus, including the basal body, MTOC ring, rootlet microtubules, and flagellar vane filaments extending ~3 µm.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citations to prior structural studies (Karpov, 2016; Pozdnyakov et al., 2017), demonstrating successful technical implementation.

results.result: Subtomogram averaging of >7500 axonemal repeats achieved 2.2 nm resolution, revealing that S. rosetta flagella contain outer dynein arms with two motor domains, the double-headed I1 inner dynein complex, and six single-headed inner dynein arms.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 are well-supported by high-resolution cryo-ET data (Figure 3, Table 1) with appropriate resolution estimates (FSC criterion), providing detailed structural characterization of dynein organization.

results.result: S. rosetta flagella exhibit doublet-specific structural features, including replacement of ODAs and IDAs on DMT 5 by o-SUB5-6 and i-SUB5-6 structures, and a unique connection between the A-tubule and IDA c on DMT 9.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15 are supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and comparison to sea urchin structures (Lin et al., 2012b), revealing conserved and unique doublet-specific features.

results.result: The positional flexibility of radial spoke heads in S. rosetta was attributed to cells being frozen while flagella were actively beating.
results.evaluation: Claim C18 is a reasonable inference from the experimental conditions (plunge-freezing of actively swimming cells) and observed structural heterogeneity, though direct evidence of beating during freezing is not provided.

results.result: S. rosetta radial spoke heads resemble narrow 'ice skate' structures similar to metazoans (sea urchin, mammals) rather than the broad structures of other unicellular species (Chlamydomonas, Tetrahymena), with RS1 and RS2 separated and RS2 and RS3 connected.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C22 are supported by high-resolution structural data (Figures 3, 4) and extensive citations to comparative studies, establishing a key evolutionary finding about radial spoke morphology.

results.result: S. rosetta flagellar doublet microtubules contain many conserved MIPs (1a, 1b, 2a, 2b, 2c, 3a, 3b, 6a-d), but unusually, MIP1a is shorter than MIP1b, contrary to other species.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 are supported by structural data (Figure 5) and comparison to prior MIP characterizations (Song et al., 2020), identifying both conserved and species-specific features.

results.result: A novel ~3.5 nm wide filamentous MIP (rail-MIP) was identified running along the A-tubule near protofilament A13, present in 39% of repeats with enrichment in DMTs 5-7, and its distribution may relate to proximal vs. distal flagellar location.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C30 are supported by classification analyses (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1-2) showing the rail-MIP's presence, distribution, and location. The proximal/distal hypothesis (C30) is speculative but supported by observational data.

results.result: S. rosetta flagella contain two additional inner junction holes beyond the typical N-DRC-related hole, located near RS1 and RS3 bases, potentially representing additional PACRG subunit losses.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 are supported by structural data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) and citations to prior work on inner junction structure (Dymek et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2019; Nicastro et al., 2011; Imhof et al., 2019). The PACRG loss interpretation (C34) is reasonable inference based on measured distances.

results.result: S. rosetta flagellar DMTs exhibit a unique ~6.5 nm gap in protofilament A2 (A2-hole), likely due to a missing tubulin dimer, present in ~39% of repeats with enrichment in DMTs 1, 5, and 6.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by classification analyses (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) showing the A2-hole's presence and distribution. The missing tubulin dimer interpretation is reasonable inference from the gap size.

results.result: The S. rosetta CPC has a relatively fixed orientation with the plane containing both microtubules roughly parallel to the 5-6 bridge, consistent with the flagellum's planar, sinusoidal waveform perpendicular to the CPC plane.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 are supported by structural data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and citations to prior work on S. rosetta flagellar beating (Dayel et al., 2011; Dayel and King, 2014), establishing CPC orientation and its functional relationship to beating.

results.result: Subtomogram averaging of >1300 CPC repeats achieved 2.5 nm resolution, revealing that S. rosetta CPC contains all major projections with periodicities of 16 nm and 32 nm, strongly resembles sea urchin CPC (lacking C2 MIP, small C1e, prominent C1a-C2a connections), but uniquely shows partial reduction of the C1d network with apparent FAP54 loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C46 are well-supported by high-resolution structural data (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Table 1) and extensive citations to comparative CPC studies (Carbajal-González et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2019; Han et al., 2022), establishing both conserved and unique CPC features.

results.result: Vane filaments were clearly observed extending from the flagellar membrane on both sides of the S. rosetta flagellum, originating at the base and extending beyond tomogram/lamella widths (~1.2-3 µm), oriented parallel to the ice layer (likely due to surface tension during blotting), consistent with predicted hydrodynamic function in filter feeding.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are supported by extensive imaging data (Figures 2, 5—figure supplement 2A, 7) and citation to modeling work (Nielsen et al., 2017). The ice layer orientation (C50) and functional interpretation (C51) are reasonable inferences from observed orientation and prior predictions.

results.result: The S. rosetta flagellar vane is composed of two sheets of thin filaments extending ~80 nm from the membrane before splitting to form diamond-shaped meshes, with 1-2 rows of nodes near the membrane where filaments branch, and the two sheets separated by ~45 nm with offset nodes.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by detailed 3D structural data (Figure 7A-D) enabling unprecedented visualization of vane architecture, including measurements of filament extension, node positions, and sheet separation.

results.result: Vane filaments showed regional variation, with some areas highly organized and interconnected while others appeared wispy, present in 53 of 54 tomograms analyzed, and also observed within the flagellar pocket at the flagellum base.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 are supported by systematic analysis across multiple tomograms (Figure 7B-D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), documenting vane structural heterogeneity and distribution.

results.result: Previously undescribed barb-like membrane complexes (~50 nm height) were identified extending from the S. rosetta flagellar membrane, consisting of a top knob, central rod with wider mid-body, and four arms connecting to the membrane. Subtomogram averaging of 600 particles with fourfold symmetry achieved 2.5 nm resolution. Barb numbers varied (0-22 per tomogram) but were consistently located near vane filament bases (median 50 nm distance). The central rod lumen is not continuous and the base appears weakly membrane-connected. Barbs were also observed in the flagellar pocket but not on co-cultured E. pacifica bacteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C68 are well-supported by high-resolution structural data (Figure 7E-K, Table 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) including subtomogram averaging, quantitative distance measurements, and systematic survey across tomograms and bacterial controls, establishing a novel flagellar structure.

results.result: The structure and organization of dyneins, radial spokes, and CPC in S. rosetta are consistent with metazoan flagella, suggesting these features were present in the urchoanozoan ancestor, pre-dating the transition to multicellularity.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are supported by comprehensive structural comparisons throughout the manuscript (Figures 3-6) showing S. rosetta's similarity to metazoans rather than other unicellular species. The evolutionary inference (C70) is reasonable based on phylogenetic position and observed structural similarities.

results.result: Most unicellular species contain three outer dynein heads per ODA while multicellular species typically contain two (consistent with genomic data showing loss in metazoans and excavates). Similarly, unicellular organisms have broad RS head structures with connections between all three heads, whereas metazoans have narrow RS heads with RS1 and RS2 separated. Metazoan CPC orientation is fixed with stable C1a-C2a connections and reduced C1e projection.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 are supported by comparative structural data (Figure 4) and extensive citations to prior structural and genomic studies (Lin et al., 2014; Nicastro et al., 2006; Pigino et al., 2012; Kollmar, 2016; Grossman-Haham et al., 2021; Gui et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2021; Carbajal-González et al., 2013), establishing key unicellular vs. multicellular differences.

results.result: Loss of bulkier flagellar structures (third dynein head, broad RS heads, larger CPC projections) may have generated space for additional molecular components in the choanoflagellate-animal ancestor. Animal cilia/flagella have adapted many additional signaling functions compared to unicellular eukaryotes. The reduced structures in S. rosetta could relate to a shift from predator avoidance to increased signaling in more stable environments, or loss of selection pressure for the third dynein head in single-flagellum organisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 are explicitly speculative ("we can speculate," "could be related") evolutionary hypotheses. While supported by citation to animal ciliary signaling functions (Bloodgood, 2010; Mitchell, 2007; Sigg et al., 2017), these remain untested hypotheses requiring additional comparative data and functional studies.

results.result: The combination of rail-MIP and A2-hole may provide strength and flexibility to compensate for loss of bulkier flagellar structures in S. rosetta. The rail-MIP may provide mechanical support to compensate for external forces such as drag from the flagellar vane.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 are speculative functional interpretations based on known MIP functions (Owa et al., 2019) and structural observations. While the rail-MIP discovery is well-supported, its proposed compensatory function and mechanical role require experimental validation through functional studies or computational modeling.

results.result: The choanoflagellate flagellar vane has been observed in only a few of >125 known species, previously described as a bilateral fringe of delicate perpendicular glycocalyx fibers extending approximately two-thirds of flagellar length. The wispy hairs observed in S. rosetta appear similar to 'partially disintegrated' vanes in Monosiga sp., suggesting they may represent a common structural variation rather than disintegration.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by citations to prior vane observations (Hibberd, 1975; Leadbeater, 2006; Mah et al., 2014) and comparison with current data. The reinterpretation of wispy structures (C85) is reasonable inference from improved preservation.

results.result: The choanoflagellate vane differs significantly from other flagellar appendages (mastigonemes, tripartite hairs). Algal mastigonemes are ~10 nm diameter with two intertwined filaments, while choanoflagellate vane filaments are ~3.5 nm arranged as wispy hairs or meshes. No connections were detected between vane filament membrane anchors and axonemal microtubules, and BLAST searches found no homologues of mastigoneme proteins MST1 and PKD2 in the S. rosetta genome.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 are supported by structural comparisons (current data vs. Liu et al., 2020; Bouck, 1971; Hibberd, 1975) and BLAST analysis results, establishing that the vane is structurally and molecularly distinct from other flagellar appendages.

results.result: The choanoflagellate vane morphology was proposed to be similar to sponge choanocyte flagellar vanes (bilateral, wing-like, membrane-anchored without axonemal connections). However, sponge choanocyte vanes appear narrower, denser, more massive, and often connect to collar microvilli. The choanoflagellate vane was previously reported to span the collar width in Monosiga brevicolis, but the current tomogram field of view did not capture vane ends to assess microvilli connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 are supported by citations to prior comparative studies (Mehl and Reiswig, 1991; Brunet and King, 2017; Hibberd, 1975; Leadbeater, 2006; Mah et al., 2014), acknowledging both similarities and differences between choanoflagellate and sponge vanes, with appropriate acknowledgment of current data limitations.

results.result: Fibers originating within the flagellar pocket suggest the vane could be secreted from the cell membrane before flagellar transport. Large fiber-filled vesicles have been observed near the apical part of choanoflagellate cells following division (when flagellum/vane would regenerate). Glycosyltransferases (jumble, couscous) localize to the basal pole and flagellar/collar base, and the collar base stains positively for lectins indicating carbohydrate chains near the flagellum. Proteinase K digest failed to remove the vane, supporting a carbohydrate or glycoprotein-based rather than proteinaceous composition.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C98 are supported by observational data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), citations to prior localization studies (Leadbeater, 2014; Wetzel et al., 2018), and experimental proteinase K digest results. The vane secretion hypothesis (C94) is reasonable inference, and the carbohydrate composition conclusion (C98) is supported by the proteinase K resistance, though the authors appropriately note additional characterization is needed.

results.result: The barbs' location alongside the vane suggests they could play a role in vane generation or maintenance. The barb top knobs resemble the size and shape of vane nodes. The S. rosetta genome has undergone extensive horizontal gene transfer from bacteria, so barbs could have ancient bacterial origin. Barb structures most closely resemble an uncharacterized bacterial complex in Prosthecobacter debontii (though with fourfold vs. fivefold symmetry).
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 are speculative functional and evolutionary hypotheses. While the structural observations (C100) and genomic context (C101, supported by Matriano et al., 2021) are valid, and the bacterial complex comparison (C102, Dobro et al., 2017) is interesting, the proposed vane-related function (C99) and bacterial origin remain untested hypotheses requiring additional evidence.

results.result: Choanoflagellate flagella more closely resemble human flagella than other protist model systems (Chlamydomonas, Tetrahymena), and may represent an attractive alternative model system for studying human ciliopathies.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 are supported by the comprehensive structural comparisons throughout the manuscript showing S. rosetta's similarity to metazoan (including human) flagella in dynein number, RS morphology, and CPC structure. The proposed utility for ciliopathy research (C104) is reasonable inference from these similarities, though explicitly speculative ("may represent").

Cryo-FIB milling was performed using a 30 keV gallium ion beam with 30 pA for initial milling/thinning and 10 pA for final polishing, producing ~150 nm lamellae. Tilt series images were collected using a K3 Summit detector at ×26,000 magnification under low-dose conditions in counting mode. The cumulative electron dose per tilt series was limited to 100 e-/Å².
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C108 are methodological details supported by the Materials and Methods section and citation to culture protocols (Levin and King, 2013). These are standard, well-documented procedures appropriate for cryo-ET studies.
